summary: Iphitus (Iphitos) of Oechalia is the son of King Eurytus who sails as an Argonaut and, in Apollodorus and related tellings, dies when Heracles hurls him from the walls of Tiryns after the Iole contest and the dispute over stolen mares. The atlas keeps a parallel node iphitus-eurytus for the Homeric bow-gift to Odysseus; ancient sources often treat one Eurytid Iphitus.
attribution: Adapted from Wikipedia, "Eurytus of Oechalia" and "Iphitos" · CC BY-SA 4.0

sections.heading: Son of Eurytus and the Argo
paragraphs: Eurytus of Oechalia, famed archer and father of Iole, numbered Iphitus among his sons. Catalogue traditions place this Iphitus with Jason's crew. When Heracles won Iole in an archery contest, Eurytus and the brothers (except Iphitus) refused the bride, fearing another outbreak of the hero's madness.

sections.heading: Death at Tiryns
paragraphs: After mares from Eurytus' herds went missing — stolen by Heracles in some tellings, by Autolycus in others — Iphitus, convinced of Heracles' innocence, sought his help and stayed as guest at Tiryns. In a fit of anger Heracles threw him from the palace walls. The murder drove Heracles into servitude under Omphale before the later sack of Oechalia and the taking of Iole.

sections.heading: Atlas dual node
paragraphs: Homer's Odyssey has Iphitus son of Eurytus give Odysseus the bow later used against the suitors. The atlas records that bow-gift strand chiefly under iphitus-eurytus while iphitus-oechalia carries the Argonaut and Tiryns-death emphasis. Both are distinct from iphitus-phocis (Naubolus' Phocian son) and from the Elean restorer of the Olympic truce.
